pages.text: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm were German scholars who, in the early nineteenth century, began collecting folk tales that had been passed down by word of mouth in German communities for generations. They published their first collection in 1812. It was not originally intended for children. It was intended as a record of German folk culture. The tales they collected were sometimes dark, violent, and strange.

image.note: Illustration: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm seated at a table with manuscripts, quill pens, and books

pages.text: Over subsequent editions, the Grimms revised the stories, softening some of the more brutal elements. Even so, Grimm's fairy tales remain more unsettling than the animated versions that most children know today. The stepmothers are genuinely cruel. The punishments for wickedness are severe. The woods are dangerous. The world is not automatically fair.

This darkness is not a flaw. It is one of the reasons these stories have survived two hundred years and been translated into more than 160 languages. Children know that the world is not always safe and fair. Stories that acknowledge this truth, while also showing how courage, kindness, and cleverness can prevail, speak to something real in their experience.

Cinderella's stepmother made her work from before dawn until after dark while her stepsisters did nothing. When the king announced a ball at which his son would choose a bride, the stepsisters went. Cinderella could not.

image.note: Illustration: Cinderella in her kitchen, stepsisters departing for the ball visible through the window

pages.text: Cinderella went to her mother's grave, where a magic tree had grown and a white bird lived that granted her wishes. She asked for a beautiful dress and shoes. She arrived at the ball. The prince danced only with her, all evening. At midnight she ran, leaving one shoe behind. The prince searched the kingdom. When the shoe was brought to Cinderella's house, the stepsisters tried to force it onto their feet, cutting their toes and heels to make it fit. It fit only Cinderella perfectly.

In the Grimm version, the stepsisters face a different kind of ending. At Cinderella's wedding, the white doves who had watched everything return to judge what they had witnessed. Each stepsister loses an eye at the church, one on the journey there and one on the return, as payment for years of cruelty. It is a harsh punishment. The Grimms did not believe in letting wickedness go unremarked.

A miller told the king that his daughter could spin straw into gold. The king locked her in a room full of straw and told her to spin it all by morning or die. She could not spin straw into gold. Nobody could. A strange little man appeared and offered to do it for her in exchange for her necklace. The next night, the king locked her in a bigger room. The little man returned, asking for her ring.

image.note: Illustration: a small, strange man at a spinning wheel, straw becoming gold thread in the lamplight

pages.text: The third night, the little man said he would spin the straw for the promise of her firstborn child. She agreed. The king married her. When her first child was born, the little man returned to claim it. She begged him to release her from the promise. He agreed on one condition: if she could guess his name within three days, she could keep the child.

On the third night, a messenger reported seeing a little man dancing around a fire in the forest, singing: 'Today I bake, tomorrow I brew, the day after that the queen's child comes in. And oh, how fortunate it is that no one knows that I am called Rumpelstiltskin!' When the queen said his name, Rumpelstiltskin tore himself in two from rage.

The Grimms collected other tales just as strange. In one, a poor miller's son inherits nothing but a cat, and is bitterly disappointed, until the cat, who can talk and walks in fine boots, sets about making his master's fortune through sheer cunning. Puss tricks a king, outwits an ogre by daring it to turn into a mouse, and wins his master a castle and a princess. The lesson, if there is one, is that brains outrank inheritance, even when the brains belong to the cat.

In another, a girl with hair long enough to climb is locked in a doorless tower by a jealous enchantress. In another, twelve princesses wear out their dancing shoes each night through a secret door no one can find. The Grimm tales are full of towers and forests, of the youngest and least regarded child winning through, of cleverness rewarded and cruelty punished. They are strange precisely because they come from a world that believed strangeness was possible.

When famine came, a woodcutter's wife persuaded him to abandon their children in the forest. The children, Hansel and Gretel, heard the plan. Hansel filled his pockets with white pebbles and left a trail home the first time. The second time, he used breadcrumbs, which the birds ate.

image.note: Illustration: Hansel and Gretel discovering the gingerbread house in the dark forest

pages.text: They found a house made of bread and cake and sugar. They began to eat. An old woman came out and invited them in. She was a witch who ate children. She locked Hansel in a cage to fatten him. She made Gretel do all the work. When the witch ordered Gretel to check whether the oven was hot enough, Gretel pretended not to understand how to do it. 'Like this,' said the witch, leaning in. Gretel pushed her in and shut the door.

Hansel and Gretel took the witch's treasure and found their way home. Their mother had died while they were gone. Their father wept to see them. The treasure was enough to sustain them. They never went hungry again.

Bruno Bettelheim, a psychologist who spent his career working with children, argued that fairy tales are not entertainment. They are therapy. A child who is afraid of being abandoned, or who feels overlooked and unfairly treated, or who is afraid of something powerful and dangerous in the adult world, finds those fears given form in fairy tales, and finds that the child in the story, the one who is small and without power, can sometimes prevail.

image.note: Illustration: a child reading a book by lamplight, the story's characters faintly visible around them

pages.text: Cinderella is not about ball gowns. It is about being unseen by the people who should see you, and being found eventually, by something or someone that recognises your worth. Hansel and Gretel is not about gingerbread. It is about discovering, when you are in the most frightening situation imaginable, that you are more capable than you knew.
The Grimms collected these stories because they were being forgotten. They survived two hundred years because children still need them. They will be needed for a while longer yet.

Why keep telling children stories with witches, wolves, and real danger in them? The Grimms would have answered that children already know the world contains danger, and that a story is a safe place to meet it. In the tale, the child faces the dark thing and, through courage or cleverness or kindness, comes through. The wolf is defeated. The lost children find their way home. The danger is real, and so is the escape.

That may be why these tales have survived two hundred years and been carried into almost every language on earth. They do not pretend life is gentle, and they do not leave the reader in despair. Between those two honesties lies their comfort. A child who has walked with Hansel and Gretel into the dark forest, and walked back out again, has rehearsed something useful: that frightening things can be survived, and that the small and powerless are not always the ones who lose.
